subtopic_detail: Screening for a mineralocorticoid excess state in resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia while the patient is already taking a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 46 year old woman whose blood pressure remains 168/104 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, all of which she takes reliably according to her dispensing record.

Her potassium has been between 3.0 and 3.3 mmol/L on three occasions over the past year, and a colleague added spironolactone 25 mg daily six weeks ago. She has no episodic sweating, palpitations or pallor. She drinks no liquorice tea and takes no over the counter preparations. Her renal function is normal and there is no bruit over either renal artery. She has never smoked and has no family history of early vascular disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg per square metre, no abdominal or flank bruit, no Cushingoid features, no radiofemoral delay, fundi with grade 1 hypertensive changes
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 4.2 mg per mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio on a morning sample later this week
options.rationale: Testing while she remains on a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is the single commonest reason this diagnosis is missed, because the drug suppresses the ratio towards normal. The near pair is that the right test is being ordered at the wrong time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request computed tomography of the adrenal glands before any blood testing
options.rationale: Imaging follows a positive biochemical screen and a confirmatory test, because non-functioning adrenal nodules are common with age and an incidental nodule on an unscreened patient invites the wrong operation. Anatomy cannot establish hormonal excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request a renal artery duplex ultrasound to assess for arterial narrowing
options.rationale: Renovascular disease is suggested by an abdominal bruit, a rise in creatinine after starting an inhibitor of the renin axis, flash pulmonary oedema, or widespread atherosclerosis. She has none of these and her renal function is normal on an inhibitor. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Hypertension)

options.text: Substitute verapamil for spironolactone and measure the ratio six weeks later
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade raises renin and can normalise the aldosterone to renin ratio, producing a false negative in precisely the patient most likely to have the condition, so it is stopped for at least six weeks and replaced with an agent that does not distort the axis, such as verapamil or prazosin. Potassium is repleted before the sample is drawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure plasma free metanephrines on a sample taken after 30 minutes supine
options.rationale: Catecholamine excess is screened for when there are paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations, labile pressure, or an adrenal mass, and it does not cause persistent hypokalaemia with alkalosis. Her symptoms are absent and her biochemistry points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Excess mineralocorticoid activity is the commonest specific cause of secondary hypertension, accounting for roughly one in ten people with hypertension and a higher proportion of those with resistant disease, yet it remains substantially underdiagnosed in Australian practice. Screening is indicated for resistant hypertension, hypertension with unexplained hypokalaemia, an adrenal incidentaloma, hypertension before the age of 40, or a family history of early stroke. The screening test is the aldosterone to renin ratio, and its interpretation depends heavily on drugs and potassium, since mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and amiloride raise renin and cause false negatives, beta blockers and clonidine lower renin and cause false positives, and inhibitors of the renin axis raise renin and can mask a positive result. Verapamil, hydralazine, prazosin and moxonidine are the agents that interfere least and are used to maintain control during the washout.
key_points: Screen resistant hypertension, especially with unexplained hypokalaemia
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists must be stopped for six weeks first
Beta blockers lower renin and produce false positive ratios
Correct hypokalaemia before sampling because it suppresses aldosterone
Imaging follows positive biochemistry, never precedes it
explanation.pearls: Hypokalaemia itself suppresses aldosterone secretion, so a patient screened while the potassium is 3.0 mmol/L can return a falsely reassuring ratio, and the potassium should be replaced into the normal range before the sample is drawn.

subtopic_detail: Negative urea breath test performed while the patient was still taking a daily proton pump inhibitor for upper abdominal burning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old man with eight months of burning upper abdominal discomfort that is worse when his stomach is empty and eases after meals. He has no dysphagia, no vomiting, no weight loss and no anaemia, and there is no family history of gastric cancer.

He bought esomeprazole over the counter and has taken 20 mg every morning for the past three months, which helps while he takes it and returns within a week of stopping. You referred him for a urea breath test, which he had four days ago while still taking the tablet, and the result has come back negative. He takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and no aspirin, and he drinks four standard drinks a week.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg per square metre, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, rectal examination not indicated with no melaena reported
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test negative taken while on a proton pump inhibitor, haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), ferritin 96 micrograms per litre (30-300), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a week of triple eradication therapy despite the negative test result
options.rationale: Treating without a positive test exposes him to two antibiotics on the basis of a result that has not been shown to be wrong, and it contributes to clarithromycin resistance. It also removes the chance of ever confirming the diagnosis cleanly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy with biopsy on the next available endoscopy list
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for alarm features such as dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, anaemia or bleeding, or for new dyspepsia over the age of 55 in Australian practice, none of which apply to him. The near pair is that biopsy would answer the question definitively but at the cost of an unnecessary procedure. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dyspepsia)

options.text: Stop the acid suppressing medication for two weeks and repeat the same test
options.rationale: Proton pump inhibitors suppress bacterial urease activity and reduce the organism load, producing false negative breath and stool antigen results, so the drug must be withheld for two weeks before testing. Repeating it off treatment is what makes the negative result interpretable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Request serology for immunoglobulin G antibodies against the organism instead
options.rationale: Antibody testing cannot distinguish current from past infection because the titre remains positive for years after eradication, which is why it is not recommended for diagnosis in Australia. It is unaffected by acid suppression but answers the wrong question. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Accept the result, label the symptoms functional and continue the current tablet
options.rationale: A functional label is made after infection has been properly excluded, and accepting a test taken under conditions known to cause false negatives closes the assessment prematurely. Long term acid suppression is then continued without a diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dyspepsia)

explanation.summary: Uninvestigated dyspepsia in a young person without alarm features is managed by testing for the organism and treating if positive, which is more cost effective than proceeding to endoscopy. The accuracy of both the urea breath test and the stool antigen test depends on conditions at the time of sampling, and false negatives follow proton pump inhibitor use within two weeks, antibiotic or bismuth use within four weeks, and recent upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Serology is not recommended because it cannot separate current from past infection. Australian first line eradication is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin twice daily for seven days, with metronidazole substituted for amoxicillin in penicillin allergy, and eradication is confirmed by a breath test at least four weeks after finishing treatment and two weeks off acid suppression.
key_points: Acid suppression within two weeks causes false negative breath and stool tests
Recent antibiotics or bismuth within four weeks do the same
Serology cannot distinguish current from past infection
Endoscopy is for alarm features or new dyspepsia over 55
Confirm eradication at least four weeks after finishing treatment
explanation.pearls: Confirmation of eradication requires the breath test to be taken at least four weeks after the last antibiotic dose and two weeks after the last proton pump inhibitor dose, and a test performed earlier than that is the usual explanation for a spurious cure.

subtopic_detail: Two centimetre segment of columnar lined lower oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia and no dysplasia on index endoscopy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the gastroenterology clinic reviewing a 54 year old man who had his first gastroscopy last month for fifteen years of reflux. The endoscopist described a 2 cm tongue of salmon coloured mucosa extending above the gastro-oesophageal junction, and four quadrant biopsies confirmed intestinal metaplasia with no dysplasia on review by a second pathologist.

His symptoms are well controlled on esomeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no dysphagia, no weight loss and no anaemia. He stopped smoking eight years ago and his body mass index is 31 kg per square metre. He has no family history of oesophageal cancer. He asks how often he will need another camera test and whether anything can remove the abnormal lining.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non-tender, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy with a 2 cm columnar lined segment above the gastro-oesophageal junction, four quadrant biopsies every 2 cm showing intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia, confirmed by a second pathologist, haemoglobin 152 g/L (130-180)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Continue acid suppression and plan repeat endoscopy in twelve months time
options.rationale: Annual endoscopy is the interval used for confirmed low grade dysplasia when ablation is declined, and the near pair matters because the presence or absence of dysplasia is what sets the interval rather than the length of the segment alone. His biopsies show no dysplasia on two pathologists' review. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance

options.text: Continue acid suppression and plan repeat endoscopy in three to five years
options.rationale: A short segment with intestinal metaplasia and no dysplasia carries an annual progression risk to cancer well under one per cent, so Australian guidance sets the surveillance interval at three to five years with ongoing acid suppression. Shorter intervals add procedures without changing outcomes at this risk level. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance

options.text: Refer for endoscopic radiofrequency ablation of the abnormal segment this year
options.rationale: Ablation is offered for confirmed low or high grade dysplasia and for intramucosal cancer, where it substantially reduces progression. Applied to metaplasia without dysplasia it exposes him to stricture and perforation risk for a very small absolute gain. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Barrett's oesophagus)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Barrett's oesophagus

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic fundoplication to prevent progression of the abnormal lining
options.rationale: Antireflux surgery controls symptoms in selected people but has not been shown to reduce progression to cancer compared with medical therapy, and it does not remove the need for surveillance. His symptoms are already controlled medically. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Barrett's oesophagus)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Barrett's oesophagus

options.text: Stop acid suppression and discharge him with no further endoscopic surveillance
options.rationale: Discharge without surveillance is appropriate when repeat biopsies show columnar mucosa without intestinal metaplasia, since that carries minimal risk. Metaplasia is present here, and stopping treatment would also return his symptoms within days. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance

explanation.summary: Columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophagus is the precursor lesion for oesophageal adenocarcinoma, but the absolute annual risk of progression in a patient without dysplasia is between 0.1 and 0.5 per cent, which is far lower than most patients assume when they hear the word precancerous. Risk rises with segment length, with male sex, with age, with obesity and above all with the grade of dysplasia, and the surveillance interval is set accordingly, from three to five years for a short non-dysplastic segment down to three monthly for untreated high grade dysplasia. Any dysplasia should be confirmed by a second expert pathologist before it drives management because interobserver agreement is poor and inflammation mimics dysplasia. Endoscopic eradication by radiofrequency ablation with resection of visible lesions has replaced oesophagectomy for dysplastic disease, and acid suppression is continued throughout.
key_points: Annual progression risk without dysplasia is well under one per cent
Segment length and dysplasia grade set the surveillance interval
Any dysplasia needs confirmation by a second expert pathologist
Ablation is for dysplastic disease, not for metaplasia alone
Antireflux surgery does not remove the need for surveillance
explanation.pearls: Columnar mucosa without intestinal metaplasia on adequate biopsies does not require ongoing surveillance under Australian guidance, so the presence or absence of goblet cells on the histology report is what decides whether the patient enters a surveillance programme at all.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Barrett's oesophagus surveillance
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Barrett's oesophagus

subtopic_detail: Two years of abdominal pain relieved by defaecation with alternating stool form, a normal faecal calprotectin and a brother with Crohn disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28 year old woman with two years of crampy lower abdominal pain that she notices most when she is stressed at work. The pain eases after she opens her bowels, and her stools swing between hard pellets and loose motions from week to week.

She has no rectal bleeding, has not lost weight and wakes at night only to pass urine. Her brother was diagnosed with Crohn disease at 22 and she is frightened she has the same thing. Her periods are regular and not painful. Examination is normal apart from mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa. Her coeliac serology is negative on a gluten containing diet and her faecal calprotectin, sent because of the family history, is 28 micrograms per gram.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, abdomen soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding, no mass, no perianal skin tags fissures or fistulae, no mouth ulcers, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin 28 micrograms per gram (less than 50), coeliac serology negative on a gluten containing diet, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies because of the family history
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for alarm features, for a raised calprotectin, or for symptoms beginning after 50, and the near pair here is that a first degree relative raises her prior probability without changing a normal calprotectin. A normal calprotectin makes inflammatory bowel disease very unlikely. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Refer for hydrogen breath testing to assess for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
options.rationale: Breath testing for overgrowth has poor reproducibility and is not recommended in routine assessment, and a positive result would not change first line management. It is reserved for specific settings such as previous bowel surgery or scleroderma. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Request computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with oral contrast medium
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is for suspected obstruction, a mass, or acute complications, none of which are suggested by a soft abdomen and normal inflammatory markers. It also delivers a substantial radiation dose to a young woman for a predictably normal result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Make the diagnosis positively and start dietary and symptom directed treatment
options.rationale: Recurrent pain related to defaecation with a change in stool form over more than six months, with no alarm features and a calprotectin under 50 micrograms per gram, meets the criteria for a positive diagnosis, and further testing lowers confidence rather than raising it. Treatment begins with dietary advice, soluble fibre and targeted antispasmodic or laxative therapy. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Start a two week course of rifaximin and review her bowel symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Poorly absorbed antibiotic therapy has a limited evidence base for the diarrhoea predominant pattern and is not funded for this indication in Australia. Prescribing it before dietary and first line measures inverts the treatment order. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Functional bowel disorder is diagnosed positively on symptom criteria rather than by excluding everything else, and the modern approach limits initial testing to a full blood count, C reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin in those under 50 without alarm features. The alarm features that redirect the assessment are rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms that wake the patient, anaemia, a palpable mass, onset after 50 and a family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease with abnormal tests. Faecal calprotectin performs well at separating functional from inflammatory disease, with a value under 50 micrograms per gram making inflammatory bowel disease unlikely. Management is stepwise, beginning with explanation, dietary modification including a supervised trial of a diet low in fermentable carbohydrates, then symptom directed drugs, with gut directed psychological therapies for refractory symptoms.
key_points: The diagnosis is made positively on symptom criteria, not by exclusion
Initial testing is limited to blood count, C reactive protein, coeliac serology and calprotectin
Calprotectin under 50 micrograms per gram makes inflammation unlikely
Nocturnal waking, bleeding and weight loss are the alarm features
A diet low in fermentable carbohydrates should be dietitian supervised
explanation.pearls: A diet low in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols should be trialled for six to eight weeks and then systematically reintroduced under dietitian supervision, because indefinite restriction narrows the diet and reduces beneficial gut bacteria without further symptom gain.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with two hours of morning stiffness and markedly raised inflammatory markers in a woman over 70 with no cranial symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74 year old woman with six weeks of aching across both shoulders and both hips that is worst on waking. She cannot lift her arms to brush her hair until she has been up for about two hours, and she needs her husband to help her out of a low chair.

She has no headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw discomfort when chewing and no visual symptoms. She has lost 2 kg and feels generally unwell. Power is normal when she is examined slowly with encouragement, and there is no swelling of the small joints of the hands. There is no rash and no proximal muscle tenderness out of proportion to the stiffness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder abduction bilaterally with full passive range, normal power against resistance once movement is initiated, no synovitis of the wrists or small joints, temporal arteries non-tender with palpable pulses, no scalp tenderness, no proximal muscle wasting
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155) with normal mean cell volume, creatine kinase 92 units per litre (less than 200), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily with clinical review within the following week
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid is the regimen for cranial arteritis, where the aim is to prevent irreversible visual loss, and the near pair matters because the two conditions overlap and are separated by cranial symptoms. She has no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual change. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

options.text: Oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid and clinical review in six weeks time
options.rationale: Methotrexate is added as a corticosteroid sparing agent for relapsing disease or for people at high risk of steroid harm, not as initial monotherapy, and it takes six to twelve weeks to work. Starting with it would leave her untreated for weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Oral naproxen twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory drugs produce at most partial relief in this condition and carry gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk in a woman of this age. A poor response also muddies the diagnostic value of the corticosteroid trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arrange temporal artery biopsy before any corticosteroid treatment is commenced
options.rationale: Biopsy is performed when cranial arteritis is suspected, and even then treatment is started immediately rather than waiting, since the histology remains positive for one to two weeks. Delaying treatment for a test that is not indicated leaves her in pain for no gain. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

options.text: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily with clinical review within the following week
options.rationale: Girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers and a normal creatine kinase in this age group responds to a moderate corticosteroid dose, and a dramatic improvement within a week both treats and supports the diagnosis. Review at one week is part of the diagnostic process rather than routine follow up. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica)

explanation.summary: Polymyalgia rheumatica is a clinical diagnosis in people over 50 with bilateral shoulder or pelvic girdle pain, morning stiffness lasting more than 45 minutes and a raised inflammatory response, and it is one of the commonest indications for long term corticosteroid in Australian general practice. The differential is wide and includes late onset rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory myopathy, hypothyroidism, bilateral rotator cuff disease, multiple myeloma and occult malignancy, which is why a normal creatine kinase, a negative rheumatoid serology and normal thyroid function are checked before committing to treatment. The response to moderate dose prednisolone is characteristically rapid and near complete within days, and a partial or absent response should prompt reconsideration rather than a dose increase. Around one in six people also develop cranial arteritis, so every review asks specifically about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms, and bone protection is planned from the outset given the expected treatment duration of one to two years.
key_points: Bilateral girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness over age 50 is the core picture
A normal creatine kinase separates this from inflammatory myopathy
Moderate dose prednisolone produces a near complete response within days
A poor response should prompt review of the diagnosis, not a higher dose
Screen for cranial symptoms at every visit and plan bone protection early
explanation.pearls: Failure to improve substantially within one week of prednisolone 15 mg daily should trigger reassessment for myeloma, malignancy or inflammatory arthritis, because a genuinely incomplete response is present in fewer than one in ten cases of this condition.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

subtopic_detail: Fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness in a man with alcohol related cirrhosis whose diagnostic ascitic tap shows a neutrophil count above the threshold with a rising creatinine
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old man with alcohol related cirrhosis and longstanding ascites who has had two days of fever and generalised abdominal discomfort. He has become slower in his responses over the same period.

He last drank alcohol four months ago. He has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no localised pain, and his abdomen is diffusely tender without guarding or rebound. He has not had an endoscopy or any instrumentation recently. A diagnostic paracentesis performed in the emergency department has just been reported. He takes spironolactone and frusemide and has never had an episode like this before.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced with mild asterixis, abdomen distended with shifting dullness and diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, no cellulitis or other visible infective focus, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear cell count 480 per cubic millimetre with no organisms seen on Gram stain, ascitic albumin 8 g/L, serum albumin 26 g/L (35-50), bilirubin 68 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.8 (0.9-1.3), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 92, white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone now and give intravenous albumin as well
options.rationale: An ascitic neutrophil count of 250 per cubic millimetre or more establishes infection of the fluid regardless of the culture result, and Australian first line treatment is a third generation cephalosporin started immediately. Albumin is added because his creatinine is above 88 micromol/L and his bilirubin above 68, which is the group in which it reduces renal failure and death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone now and withhold albumin pending the culture
options.rationale: The antibiotic choice is right but omitting albumin in a patient who meets the renal and hepatic criteria discards a treatment shown to reduce hepatorenal failure and mortality. The near pair matters because albumin is not given to everyone, only to those with impaired renal or hepatic markers. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Ascites)

options.text: Start oral norfloxacin now and arrange a repeat paracentesis in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral quinolone is the regimen for secondary prophylaxis after an episode has been treated, or for primary prophylaxis in low protein ascites, not for an acute episode with sepsis physiology. He is hypotensive and tachycardic and needs intravenous treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a large volume therapeutic paracentesis now with albumin replacement
options.rationale: Large volume drainage relieves tense ascites causing respiratory compromise, and his distension is not the acute problem. Draining infected fluid does not treat the infection and delays the antibiotic that does. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Ascites)

options.text: Await ascitic fluid culture results before committing to any antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Cultures are negative in around 40 per cent of genuine episodes, so waiting for them would leave many patients untreated, and mortality rises sharply with delay. The neutrophil count is the diagnostic criterion, not the culture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgically treatable source occurs in a substantial minority of cirrhotic patients admitted with ascites and carries a mortality of 20 to 30 per cent even when treated. It presents non-specifically with fever, abdominal pain, worsening encephalopathy, renal impairment or simply clinical deterioration, so any cirrhotic patient with ascites who deteriorates gets a diagnostic tap before antibiotics. The diagnosis rests on an ascitic polymorphonuclear count of 250 per cubic millimetre or more, and culture in blood culture bottles at the bedside improves yield but remains negative in many cases. Intravenous albumin at 1.5 g per kg on day one and 1 g per kg on day three reduces hepatorenal syndrome and death in those with a creatinine above 88 micromol/L, urea above 10.7 mmol/L or bilirubin above 68 micromol/L. After recovery, long term quinolone prophylaxis is indicated and the patient should be assessed for transplantation.
key_points: A tap before antibiotics is mandatory in any deteriorating cirrhotic with ascites
A neutrophil count of 250 or more makes the diagnosis regardless of culture
Culture is negative in around 40 per cent of genuine episodes
Albumin reduces renal failure and death in those with impaired renal or hepatic markers
Secondary quinolone prophylaxis follows every treated episode
explanation.pearls: A neutrophil count at or above 250 per cubic millimetre with more than one organism on Gram stain, a protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L or a raised lactate dehydrogenase suggests a perforated viscus instead, and that combination needs urgent imaging and a surgical opinion rather than antibiotics alone.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, medical

subtopic_detail: Three centimetre adrenal nodule with low unenhanced attenuation found incidentally on imaging for renal colic in a normotensive man
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old man who had a computed tomogram last week for left sided loin pain. He passed a 4 mm stone and the pain has settled, but the report also describes a 3 cm nodule in the right adrenal gland with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and a smooth margin.

He feels well. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure today is normal, and he has had no episodes of sweating, headache or palpitations. He has not gained weight, has no striae and no proximal weakness, and there is no easy bruising. He has never had a cancer diagnosis and has never smoked. His potassium and renal function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, no supraclavicular fat pad, no purple striae, no proximal myopathy, no hirsutism, no palpable abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography showing a 3 cm right adrenal nodule with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and smooth margins, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule to obtain a tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy of an adrenal nodule before catecholamine excess has been excluded can provoke a hypertensive crisis, and it cannot distinguish an adenoma from an adrenocortical carcinoma in any case. It is reserved for suspected metastasis in a patient with a known primary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic adrenalectomy because the nodule measures more than 3 cm
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for a functioning nodule or for radiological features suggesting malignancy, with size thresholds usually set around 4 cm alongside those features. A smooth 3 cm lesion with low attenuation has benign imaging characteristics. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adrenal incidentaloma)

options.text: Screen for hormone excess with an overnight dexamethasone test and metanephrines
options.rationale: Every adrenal nodule found incidentally needs assessment of whether it secretes, and the minimum screen is a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test for cortisol excess and plasma free or urinary metanephrines for catecholamine excess, with an aldosterone to renin ratio added only if there is hypertension or hypokalaemia. Both of his relevant clinical prompts are absent, but function still has to be excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat the computed tomogram in twelve months with no biochemical testing now
options.rationale: Imaging follow up alone misses the subclinical cortisol excess that is present in a meaningful minority and that carries measurable cardiovascular and bone consequences. The near pair is that surveillance is part of the plan but never a substitute for the functional screen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the nodule before further testing
options.rationale: Functional imaging is used when the lesion has indeterminate attenuation or when metastatic disease is suspected, since it addresses malignancy rather than hormone secretion. Attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units already indicates a lipid rich benign lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adrenal incidentaloma)

explanation.summary: Adrenal nodules are found on around four per cent of abdominal computed tomograms and the proportion rises with age, so the practical question is never whether the lesion is there but whether it secretes and whether it is malignant. Unenhanced attenuation answers most of the malignancy question, since a value at or below 10 Hounsfield units indicates a lipid rich adenoma with a very high negative predictive value, while higher attenuation, irregular margins, size above 4 cm and rapid growth all raise concern. The functional question is answered biochemically in every case, because mild autonomous cortisol secretion is frequently present without any of the classical physical signs and is associated with hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis and increased mortality. Catecholamine excess must be excluded before any biopsy or operation, and mineralocorticoid screening is added when there is hypertension or hypokalaemia.
key_points: Attenuation of 10 Hounsfield units or less indicates a lipid rich adenoma
Every incidental nodule needs a functional screen regardless of symptoms
Mild autonomous cortisol secretion occurs without classical physical signs
Exclude catecholamine excess before any biopsy or operation
Mineralocorticoid screening is added only with hypertension or hypokalaemia
explanation.pearls: A serum cortisol above 50 nanomoles per litre the morning after 1 mg of dexamethasone indicates failure of suppression, and this finding in an apparently asymptomatic patient predicts a higher rate of vertebral fracture and cardiovascular events over the following decade.
